headline: Peanut Bunker Push the Ledges, Bonito Hit Point Judith, Albies Knock on the Breachways
subhead: Bait is stacking tight to the rocks from Second Beach to Napatree, and the first false albacore and bonito of the season are working their way toward the breachway mouths.
body_markdown:
Peanut bunker have been working down the ledges all week, tight to the rocks from Second Beach through Sachuest and around to Sakonnet Point, getting pushed and balled up by whatever's chasing them on the last two hours of the ebb. That bait movement is the story right now. It's what pulled the first bonito into Point Judith and Block Island in real numbers this week, and it's the same signal that has guys at Watch Hill and Napatree watching the breachway mouths a little closer than usual, because this is exactly the calendar window when albies start pushing into Charlestown, Quonnie, and Weekapaug on the morning tide.

We flagged this last week — said to expect steady, incremental improvement in the surf striper bite over the next several days — and the peanut bunker piling up along the ledges is backing that up. It's not a blitz yet. It's schoolies and a scattering of slot fish working the wash at first light and again at dusk, but the bait density is building the way it's supposed to this time of year, and that's the trigger everyone's waiting on for the real fall push to start.

Water's still warm for the season, running in the high 60s to low 70s depending on where you check, which keeps things in a holding pattern rather than an explosion. Bonito and albies like that kind of water, which is exactly why Point Judith before the Sakonnet side did — that structure sits a little further out, catches cleaner water off the reef, and the bait doesn't have to travel as far. Expect that push to keep spreading west over the next several days to two weeks as the pattern usually goes, which means Sakonnet Point, Second Beach, and the Newport ledges should start seeing scattered fish before the breachways do, and Watch Hill and Napatree picking it up last as the bait finally works its way down the south shore and funnels into those inlets.

On the bonito, the Point Judith and Block Island contingent is working small profile stuff — half-ounce epoxy jigs, Deadly Dicks, and Albie Snax in bone or pearl, worked fast on light fluoro, 15 to 20 pound leader, because these fish are locked onto tiny bait and won't touch anything that doesn't match the hatch. Same story creeping into Nantucket Sound with the albies — showing but finicky, feeding on something small enough that standard-size Deceivers are getting refused. If you're marking bait but not getting bit, downsize before you do anything else.

Striper fishing off the rocks is honest work right now, not a guarantee. The better window is that last hour of light into full dark, working white bucktails or three-inch swim shads through the pockets between the ledges at Beavertail, off the rocks below the Newport bridge, and along the Sachuest side. Incoming tide is pushing bait into those pockets and the fish are using the moving water to pin it against structure, so time your casts to the current, not the clock. A few better fish are coming on bunker chunks fished at night off the deeper Newport ledges, but daytime action is mostly schoolies and short slot fish mixed in with the peanut bunker.

Bluefish remain the most dependable player on the whole south shore. Choppers are working the bunker schools hard off Second Beach and around Sakonnet Point, and that activity should keep tracking with bait density straight through Labor Day week — wherever the bunker are thick, the blues are on them. Tin squids and single-hook poppers on wire leader are doing the damage; no finesse required, just get something shiny in front of them.

Fluke have settled into the pattern we called for — fair, not great, holding on structure and in the deeper channels rather than collapsing outright. The breachway channel edges at Charlestown and Quonnie are still giving up keeper fish on white Gulp paired with quarter-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom on the last of the ebb when the water's pulling out through the cut. Jamestown's deeper holes off the west side are producing similarly — slow and steady beats aggressive jigging right now. Expect that fair-to-good pattern to hold through September before the fish start their move offshore.

On the blackfish side, it's early yet, but there's a feeler bite starting to show on the deeper ledges off Beavertail and around Fort Wetherill as water starts its seasonal cool. Nothing worth planning a trip around yet, but rock hoppers who like to be ahead of the season should start scouting which cracks are holding crabs on the slack tide, because that bite only gets better from here into October.

Looking ahead, the next several days should bring more of the same trend — bait continuing to concentrate along the ledges, bonito holding steady or building at Point Judith and Block Island, and the first real test of whether albies commit to the breachways before the moon builds toward full and tidal flow picks up. If the bait keeps pushing west the way it typically does this time of year, Watch Hill and Napatree are worth checking daily starting this weekend. Keep a Plan B on the striper side — the schoolie bite is real but not blitz-caliber yet, and it likely won't be until the bunker schools in Narragansett Bay get squeezed tighter by the tide.
